messages.content: I want to design a distributed scheduler for preemptible gang jobs. It needs to reconcile tenant fairness with placement constraints and recover from scheduler partitions. What are the central requirements?

The design has two requirements to satisfy together. It must prevent conflicting resource assignments during partitions, including assignments attempted by stale schedulers and conflicts involving partially completed gang reservations. Once connectivity stabilizes, it must restore scheduling progress within 30 seconds while preventing starvation under feasible demand. Tenant fairness, placement constraints, and the fact that jobs are both preemptible and gang-scheduled all shape how those requirements can be met.
Why does gang scheduling make the partition problem different from assigning one task at a time?

A gang needs a compatible collection of resources to run together. During a partition, a scheduler might reserve only part of that collection before losing contact with other components. Those partial reservations cannot simply be treated as a successful gang placement. But they also cannot be ignored if another scheduler could still regard them as valid: doing so could produce conflicting assignments. The design therefore has to account for the in-between state, not just completed placements and completely free resources.
If schedulers each maintain their own view of free resources, could they keep making assignments while disconnected?

A local view alone would not establish that an assignment is safe. Two disconnected schedulers could each see the same resource as available, or one could act on an outdated view after another has gained authority to assign it. A design may allow work to proceed where it can establish exclusive authority, but the safety requirement does not permit conflicting assignments merely to preserve activity during a partition. The exact mechanism for establishing that authority is a design choice; the exclusion property is the requirement.
What should happen if a stale scheduler sends an assignment after the partition begins to heal?

That assignment must not conflict with one made under current authority. Merely informing the stale scheduler that its view is outdated may be insufficient if it has an in-flight action. Conceptually, the design needs a way for an assignment to be accepted only when the scheduler is still entitled to make it. Fencing old authority is one possible pattern to examine, but what matters here is the observable guarantee: a stale scheduler cannot cause a conflicting resource assignment.
And how should I reason about a reservation that has completed for only part of a gang?

Treat it as a state that needs explicit safety handling. The reserved resources might still be claimed, while the gang as a whole is not yet ready to run. The scheduler must neither count the partial reservation as a completed placement nor reassign its resources incompatibly while that claim might remain valid. It also needs a safe path toward either a coherent gang placement or making the resources available again. Those are conceptual obligations, not a prescribed reservation protocol.
Could I just release every incomplete gang reservation when a partition is detected?

Only if release can be established safely. Detection by one component does not necessarily mean another component has stopped acting on the reservation or on an earlier assignment. Declaring resources free too early could recreate the conflicting-assignment problem. On the other hand, leaving partial reservations unresolved indefinitely could obstruct placement and scheduling progress. The design has to handle both risks without assuming that every participant learns about a partition at the same moment.
Does the fact that the jobs are preemptible make resource conflicts less serious?

No. Preemptibility means a running job can, subject to the scheduler's rules, give way to other work. It does not make two incompatible assignments of the same resource safe. Preemption may help the scheduler find a placement or address fairness, but a transition away from a preempted job still has to respect the assignment-safety requirement. The problem does not specify a particular preemption policy or say that preemption by itself resolves partition recovery.
How do tenant fairness and placement constraints fit together? A tenant might be due an opportunity but have a gang that cannot fit.

Fairness has to be considered alongside what can actually be placed. Favoring a tenant in an abstract ordering does not create a valid placement for its gang, and repeatedly favoring only easy-to-place work could starve feasible demand from another tenant. The design needs to distinguish a placement that is currently infeasible from one that is feasible but keeps losing opportunities. No particular fairness formula, tenant weighting, or placement rule is specified, so those choices remain open.
What does 'preventing starvation under feasible demand' require me to watch for?

It rules out a pattern in which demand that can be served is indefinitely bypassed as the scheduler continues making other placements. For gang jobs, feasibility must take the whole gang and its placement constraints into account; having a few available resources is not necessarily enough. Fairness decisions, preemption, and lingering reservations can all affect whether feasible demand gets an opportunity. The requirement does not supply a separate per-job waiting-time bound, and it does not promise service for demand that cannot feasibly be placed.
Is the 30-second requirement a deadline for every queued gang to start?

No. The stated requirement is to restore scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. That is different from completing recovery of every reservation, starting every queued gang, or satisfying every tenant within 30 seconds. At the same time, progress cannot be pursued by allowing conflicting assignments, and the scheduler still has to prevent starvation under feasible demand. The precise measure of 'scheduling progress' would need to be made clear in a design, without silently turning this requirement into a deadline for every job.
Why is the phrase 'after connectivity stabilizes' important?

It identifies when the 30-second recovery condition applies. During an ongoing partition, some schedulers may lack the information or authority needed to make safe assignments. Once connectivity is stable, the design must be able to resume scheduling progress within that stated interval. It should not depend on treating an intermittently connected system as though all participants have already converged, nor should it confuse the time of partition detection with the specified starting condition.
Could a conservative safety rule end up conflicting with the recovery and fairness goals?

Yes, if it prevents conflicts by leaving resources unavailable indefinitely even after they can safely be reconciled. The three concerns have to be evaluated together: no conflicting assignments during partitions, progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes, and no starvation under feasible demand. A safe pause while authority is uncertain is different from a system that cannot regain progress once that uncertainty can be resolved. Partial gang reservations are particularly important because they can impede both placement and fairness if they remain unresolved.
What would a useful design review focus on without assuming a specific scheduling algorithm?

It could trace the points at which resource claims become effective, lose authority, or become available again. For each point, ask whether a stale scheduler or an incomplete gang reservation could still produce a conflicting assignment. Then examine how the scheduler finds placements consistent with gang requirements, how it gives tenants fair opportunities when their demand is feasible, and how it resumes progress within 30 seconds of stable connectivity. That review checks the stated properties without presuming a particular fairness formula, coordination mechanism, or recovery procedure.
So I should not treat safety during a partition and progress afterward as separate problems?

Right. They are distinct properties but interact. A partition-safe design needs to know when an assignment is authoritative even if schedulers disagree; a recovering design needs to reconcile uncertain or partial claims without assigning their resources twice. Once connectivity stabilizes, that reconciliation must not prevent scheduling progress beyond 30 seconds. Throughout, placement constraints and tenant fairness still matter, especially so that feasible demand does not starve while the scheduler resumes normal activity.

For the distributed scheduler, I propose quorum-fenced scheduler epochs, worker-verified atomic gang commits, tenant-weighted aging with constraint-aware preemption, and five-second failover leases. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the design. Quorum-fenced epochs are intended to distinguish a scheduler with current authority from a stale one. Worker verification makes that distinction matter at the point where a resource assignment takes effect. Atomic gang commits address the risk that a partly reserved gang is mistaken for a complete placement. Tenant-weighted aging and constraint-aware preemption bring fairness and feasible placement into scheduling decisions. Five-second failover leases are a proposed way to limit how long failed scheduler authority persists. The pieces form a proposal, not yet a demonstration that the safety, 30-second recovery, and starvation requirements are met.
What work is the quorum doing in a quorum-fenced epoch?

Conceptually, it prevents independent schedulers from each treating their own unsupported claim of authority as sufficient. A scheduler obtains an epoch through the quorum mechanism, and fencing distinguishes its authority from that of a scheduler operating under an older epoch. For the proposal to prevent conflicts, the quorum arrangement and the checks on assignments must actually exclude incompatible authority. Giving epochs names alone would not provide that guarantee.
Suppose a scheduler was active before a partition and keeps sending assignments afterward. Where should the fencing take effect?

The proposal calls for workers to verify the authority relevant to an assignment, rather than trusting a scheduler's local view. An action from the stale scheduler must not become an effective conflicting resource assignment just because its message eventually arrives. Verification at the worker is important because a scheduler can continue sending messages after other components have moved on. The proposal still needs precise rules for what a worker verifies and for which actions require verification.
Does checking an epoch at the worker automatically make a gang commit atomic?

No. Epoch verification addresses whether an action comes from valid scheduler authority; gang atomicity addresses whether the collection of resource claims becomes one coherent placement. A set of individually authorized worker decisions could still leave a gang only partly reserved. 'Worker-verified atomic gang commits' therefore needs both properties: workers reject actions that lack valid authority, and an incomplete collection of reservations is not exposed as a committed gang placement.
What should I say about those incomplete reservations without choosing a commit protocol yet?

Say that they remain a distinct state requiring safe resolution. While a partial reservation might still be valid, its resources must not be assigned incompatibly elsewhere. At the same time, the scheduler must not treat that partial reservation as a successfully committed gang. The proposal requires a way to reach a coherent commit or make the claims available again safely; it does not, by itself, specify the messages or storage mechanism that accomplishes this.
Could workers just each confirm their portion and let the gang start as confirmations arrive?

That would need careful qualification. If confirmations make individual portions independently usable before the whole gang is committed, the placement may no longer be atomic in the sense the proposal needs. The worker confirmations could be part of verification, but the design would still need a clear point at which the gang as a whole is committed and a safe interpretation of any confirmations that arrive before that point.
How does the five-second failover lease relate to the epoch?

The lease is the proposed time-bounded aspect of failover authority; the epoch is the proposed fencing distinction between authorities. They need compatible semantics. In particular, expiration or replacement of a lease must not leave a former scheduler able to create effective conflicting assignments, and gaining a new epoch must not silently make existing worker claims safe to reuse. 'Five-second failover leases' states a duration, but not yet the exact renewal, expiration, or worker-verification rules.
Is a five-second lease enough on its own to show that scheduling resumes within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes?

No. Five seconds is the proposed lease duration; 30 seconds is the required bound for restoring scheduling progress after connectivity stabilizes. Failover, establishing valid authority, reconciling partial gang reservations, and finding a permissible placement all bear on progress. The lease duration may be relevant to that analysis, but it is not itself a proof of the 30-second requirement.
Would shortening the lease necessarily improve recovery?

Not necessarily. A shorter lease changes how frequently authority may need to be maintained or re-established, but it does not by itself resolve uncertain gang reservations or placement constraints. It could also affect how often the system must handle authority transitions. The stated proposal is for five-second failover leases; whether that duration supports the required recovery behavior has to be assessed with the rest of the design.
Can a partitioned scheduler keep working if it cannot reach the quorum?

It cannot safely create assignments merely on the strength of an isolated local view if doing so could conflict with assignments made elsewhere. The proposal's quorum fencing is meant to constrain authority during that situation. Exactly which work, if any, can proceed depends on the authority and worker-verification rules the design establishes. Safety during the partition takes precedence over treating every disconnected scheduler as independently entitled to assign resources.
Now for fairness: what does tenant-weighted aging contribute?

It proposes that tenant weight and time spent waiting both affect scheduling opportunities. Aging is meant to keep a tenant's feasible demand from being overlooked indefinitely as other work is considered. But the phrase does not specify a scoring formula or prove starvation freedom. In particular, the scheduler still has to account for whether the tenant's gang can satisfy its placement constraints; increasing priority cannot make an infeasible placement valid.
Why pair aging with constraint-aware preemption rather than preempting whenever a tenant's priority rises?

For a gang job, removing some running work helps only if it can lead to a valid placement for the gang under its constraints. Constraint-aware preemption asks the scheduler to consider that placement question rather than preempting solely because a priority value has risen. It also avoids treating preemption as an exception to assignment safety: resources cannot be reassigned incompatibly while their prior claims still apply. The proposal does not yet choose a particular preemption threshold or selection rule.
Could weighting itself cause starvation?

The risk to examine is whether the combined weighting, aging, placement, and preemption behavior can indefinitely bypass feasible demand. Tenant weights can influence relative opportunities, but the requirement remains to prevent starvation under feasible demand. Stating that the policy includes aging is not enough; the design would need to show that a feasible tenant does not keep losing every opportunity despite waiting.
How would placement constraints affect that assessment?

A waiting gang may need a particular combination of resources. Its wait cannot be evaluated solely by counting idle capacity or comparing tenant scores; the scheduler has to consider whether a placement satisfying the gang's constraints is feasible. Conversely, it should not label demand infeasible simply because an inconvenient current allocation has never been reconsidered, especially when preemption is part of the proposal. The assessment has to connect fairness decisions to actual placement opportunities.
If a gang's reservation is partially complete when failover occurs, which of these mechanisms is responsible?

Several interact. Epoch fencing and worker verification prevent an old scheduler from making new effective conflicting claims. Atomic gang-commit semantics determine why a partial reservation is not yet a completed placement and how its claims remain protected. Failover leases affect the transition between scheduler authorities. Fairness and preemption matter once the resources' usable state is known and scheduling can proceed. None of those mechanisms should assume that lease expiration alone makes every partially reserved resource immediately free.
What is the most important boundary between the scheduler's decision and a worker's action?

A scheduler deciding that a placement is desirable is not the same as workers accepting an effective assignment. The proposal puts verification at workers so that stale scheduler decisions cannot become conflicting assignments, while the gang-commit rule must prevent individually accepted pieces from being mistaken for an all-or-nothing placement. That boundary is where authority and gang completeness both need to be meaningful, rather than existing only in the scheduler's calculations.
Should I describe this as guaranteeing safe recovery and fairness?

Describe it as a proposed design aimed at those requirements, not as an established guarantee. The specific mechanisms are quorum-fenced scheduler epochs, worker-verified atomic gang commits, tenant-weighted aging with constraint-aware preemption, and five-second failover leases. To substantiate the claim, the design would need to show that stale schedulers and partial reservations cannot produce conflicting assignments, that scheduling progress returns within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes, and that feasible demand does not starve.
What questions remain about the five-second lease in particular?

The design needs to clarify what authority the lease covers, what happens when it expires or is replaced, and what workers accept during that transition. It also needs to account for a lease holder that has sent actions which have not yet reached workers, and for gang reservations that are incomplete at failover. Those questions follow from the proposed lease and the safety requirement; they do not change the specified five-second duration.
And the unresolved question for atomic commits is whether the entire gang becomes valid together, despite failures partway through?

Yes. The key distinction is between collecting tentative claims and making an effective placement for the entire gang. A failure partway through must not leave a partial gang treated as committed or allow its still-valid claims to be reassigned in conflict. The proposal names worker-verified atomic gang commits as the approach, while the exact method for coordinating that all-or-nothing outcome remains to be defined.
How do workers identify and release partial gang reservations when a scheduler loses its lease mid-commit?

They need to distinguish a reservation for a particular gang from an effective assignment for that gang. A worker would need enough information with its claim to identify the gang, the scheduler authority under which the claim was made, and whether the claim is still tentative or has reached a valid commit outcome. Lease loss is a reason to reconcile a tentative claim, but it is not, by itself, proof that the entire gang failed to commit or that the resource is safe to reassign.
Why can't each worker release its own reservation as soon as it notices that the scheduler's lease has expired?

Each worker may see only its portion of a commit in progress. Its local observation of lease expiry does not tell it whether the gang reached a valid commit outcome elsewhere, or whether an earlier message remains in flight. If it frees the resource and another assignment takes effect while the original claim can still become effective, the safety requirement is at risk. Release needs to be tied to an authoritative outcome and to fencing of actions that could revive the old claim.
So how would a worker recognize that two tentative claims are parts of the same gang?

The claims need a common gang identity, together with a way to distinguish one placement attempt from another and associate each claim with its scheduler authority. Otherwise, workers could mistake claims from separate attempts for one commit, or fail to recognize which tentative claims need reconciliation together. That describes the information the design must make available; it does not prescribe a particular identifier format or message protocol.
Does a worker need to know where every other member of the gang was reserved?

Not necessarily from its own local state. What it does need is a reliable way to determine whether its claim belongs to a gang that committed or to an attempt that can safely be abandoned. A worker's local claim alone cannot establish that all the other claims exist and have the same outcome. The design could make the collective outcome verifiable without giving every worker an independent, complete view of every placement decision.
If some workers have acknowledged reservations and others have not, what state is the gang in?

It is still an incomplete attempt unless the rules for an atomic gang commit have been satisfied. Acknowledging a tentative reservation is not the same as declaring the entire gang placed. The acknowledged resources may need to remain protected while the outcome is uncertain, but the gang must not be treated as running merely because some of its workers responded.
What evidence would justify releasing those acknowledged reservations?

Conceptually, the worker needs evidence that the attempt will not become a valid committed placement, plus assurance that messages from the lease-losing scheduler cannot later make its old claim effective. An authoritative abort or an equivalent conclusively failed outcome could supply the first part, depending on the eventual design. Fencing supplies the second part. Without both, 'I have not heard a commit yet' is weaker than 'this attempt cannot commit.'
Could a new scheduler decide the old attempt failed and tell the workers to release it?

That could be part of a design if the new scheduler has established the authority to resolve the old attempt and workers can verify its instruction. It must first distinguish an uncertain partial reservation from a gang that validly committed. Merely having a new scheduler, or observing that the old lease ended, does not make an unsupported release decision safe.
What if a commit message from the old scheduler arrives after the release instruction?

The worker must not let that delayed message restore the old claim or create an assignment that conflicts with a newer one. This is where fencing has to apply to commit actions, not just to initial reservations. The rules for accepting a release and for accepting a commit need a consistent ordering of authority; otherwise a worker could release a resource and then accept a late instruction to commit it again.
Could a worker instead keep the reservation until it receives a definite answer?

That is the safer response while the outcome is genuinely uncertain, provided the worker does not treat the tentative claim as a completed gang assignment. But retaining uncertain reservations without a timely way to resolve them can block placements. The design must reconcile that conservative behavior with the requirement to restore scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. The lease duration alone does not settle the reservation's outcome.
Would the five-second failover lease make an unresolved reservation expire after five seconds?

The proposal specifies a five-second failover lease, but it has not said that gang reservations share that expiry or may be released at that moment. A scheduler losing authority and a worker safely freeing a particular resource are different events. Treating them as identical would require rules showing that no valid commit remains possible and no stale message can reestablish the claim.
What if a worker believes the gang committed just before the lease was lost, while another still sees only a tentative reservation?

That is exactly the kind of disagreement the commit rule must resolve. The workers cannot independently choose outcomes that make one portion an effective gang assignment and another portion freely reassignable. They need a verifiable collective outcome for the attempt, even if they learn it at different times. Until that outcome can be established, the worker with the uncertain claim must avoid an incompatible reassignment.
Does 'atomic' mean all workers must learn the outcome at exactly the same instant?

No. It means the effective placement must have a coherent all-or-nothing outcome, rather than leaving an accepted partial gang. Workers may learn about that outcome at different times, which is why their handling of tentative claims, late messages, and release must remain safe during the interval. Simultaneous observation is not the requirement; avoiding conflicting or partial effective assignments is.
How does a worker distinguish an abandoned partial reservation from a committed gang that later gets preempted?

They have different starting states. An abandoned partial reservation never becomes a valid full-gang placement and needs safe cleanup. A committed gang has an effective assignment; preemption is a subsequent change to that assignment. Workers need to verify the relevant authority and transition in either case, but they should not infer that a committed assignment is merely tentative because the scheduler that initiated it later lost its lease.
Is it enough to prevent the old scheduler from making new reservations, while allowing its earlier commit messages through?

Not without accounting for how those earlier messages interact with reconciliation. An in-flight commit message can be decisive even though it was sent before lease loss. The design must define whether and when it can still take effect, and ensure that workers do not both release the attempt for reuse and accept a commit that conflicts with that reuse. Fencing only new reservations would leave that race unanswered.
What is the central question each worker has to answer before making a resource available again?

Whether its particular claim is conclusively no longer needed for a valid gang assignment and cannot be made effective by stale authority. Identifying the gang and placement attempt tells the worker which claim is under discussion; a verifiable outcome and fencing determine whether release is safe. Once released, the worker must treat delayed actions consistently with that decision so the same resource cannot be assigned incompatibly.
So lease loss should trigger reconciliation, not an automatic local rollback?

Yes—that is the key distinction to preserve in the design. Mid-commit lease loss leaves the status of some gang claims uncertain until the workers can verify a coherent outcome. Reconciliation must identify those claims, protect them against conflicting reuse while uncertain, and release them only when the old attempt cannot validly commit. It also needs to finish promptly enough after connectivity stabilizes to support scheduling progress within 30 seconds, without letting feasible demand starve.

My hypothesis is that epoch-fenced workers expiring uncommitted gang-ID reservations after five seconds will clear orphaned holds within ten seconds without conflicting assignments. Does that answer the mid-commit lease-loss question?

It offers a specific possible answer, but it remains a hypothesis. Gang IDs give workers a way to identify the reservations in question; the five-second expiry is the proposed release rule; and epoch fencing is intended to prevent stale scheduler actions from turning released resources into conflicting assignments. The claim to establish is that orphaned holds clear within ten seconds while assignment safety is preserved, including when a lease is lost mid-commit.
Why isn't the five-second expiry enough to establish the ten-second claim?

An expiry rule and an observed clearance bound are different claims. The hypothesis needs to say when the five seconds start, when an orphaned hold counts as cleared, and what event starts the ten-second interval. It also needs to account for how a worker determines that a reservation is uncommitted. Without those meanings, the two numbers are specific but do not yet show that the stated outcome follows.
Isn't a reservation uncommitted whenever that worker hasn't received a commit?

That may describe the worker's local knowledge, but it does not necessarily establish the gang's outcome. A commit might be in flight, or the worker might not yet have learned an authoritative outcome for the attempt. The hypothesis depends on expiring *uncommitted* gang-ID reservations, so the distinction between 'no commit observed here' and 'this attempt cannot validly commit' matters for avoiding conflicting assignments.
Then what does the gang ID contribute?

It identifies which gang a reservation belongs to, so a worker can distinguish that tentative claim from unrelated resource claims. For mid-commit cleanup, the worker also needs to avoid confusing separate attempts involving the same gang. Whether the gang ID alone provides enough distinction depends on what it identifies in the eventual design; the hypothesis does not specify that detail.
If the reservation expires, couldn't the worker simply mark its resource free?

That is the proposed effect of expiry, but marking the resource free is safe only if an old action cannot subsequently make the expired reservation effective. Epoch fencing must apply at the points where a delayed reservation or commit action could change the worker's assignment state. Otherwise, the worker could free a resource, accept a new assignment, and later accept an incompatible action associated with the old gang.
Would rejecting actions from older epochs settle that?

It addresses a central part of the risk: actions from a scheduler whose epoch has been superseded must not create effective conflicting claims. The hypothesis also needs coherent treatment of the reservation that was already accepted and of any commit action associated with it. A worker cannot rely on expiry for release while allowing a late action to revive the same claim incompatibly. Whether epoch fencing settles every such case depends on its precise acceptance rules.
Could expiry happen while the scheduler still believes the gang is committing?

That possibility has to be considered. A worker's five-second timer and a scheduler's view of the commit might not yield the same conclusion at the same instant. The proposed rule needs to ensure that expiry and any valid commit outcome cannot produce a partly effective gang or conflicting use of a resource. Calling a reservation uncommitted is not enough unless the rule makes its eventual outcome unambiguous.
What if only some of the workers expire their reservations?

Then the hypothesis has to handle a mixed view of the same gang. The expired claims must not be revived incompatibly, and the claims that remain held must not be mistaken for a fully committed placement merely because they did not expire. The safety question is about the entire gang attempt, even though each worker may observe and act on its own reservation at a different time.
Does 'atomic gang commit' require all the workers' five-second timers to expire together?

No. Workers need not observe an outcome simultaneously. What matters is that differing observation times do not yield a valid partial gang or conflicting assignments. The hypothesis needs to make expiry consistent with the all-or-nothing commit outcome; synchronized timers are not stated as part of it.
When should I call a hold orphaned?

For this hypothesis, the useful distinction is between a reservation still needed for a valid gang commit and one left behind without a valid path to becoming that commit. Calling a hold 'orphaned' should not substitute for establishing which of those situations applies. Otherwise, the ten-second clearance claim could appear satisfied simply by classifying uncertain holds as orphans and freeing them prematurely.
Does the ten-second claim mean ten seconds after connectivity stabilizes?

The hypothesis says 'within ten seconds' but does not specify its starting event. Connectivity stabilization is the starting condition for the separate requirement to restore scheduling progress within 30 seconds. It would be important to define the ten-second clock explicitly rather than assume it shares that starting point, or assume it starts when a worker detects lease loss.
If orphaned holds clear within ten seconds, would that establish scheduling progress within 30 seconds?

Not by itself. Clearing holds may remove an obstacle to placement, but progress also depends on valid scheduling authority and on finding placements that satisfy gang and tenant constraints. The ten-second statement concerns orphaned holds; the 30-second requirement concerns restored scheduling progress after connectivity stabilizes. Both matter, but one does not automatically prove the other.
And does quick expiry establish that feasible tenant demand won't starve?

No. Quick cleanup can keep abandoned reservations from blocking feasible placements indefinitely, which is relevant to starvation. But preventing starvation also depends on which feasible demand the scheduler chooses to serve over time, including its tenant-fairness and placement decisions. The hypothesis makes a clearance-and-safety claim, not a standalone fairness guarantee.
How would I examine the 'without conflicting assignments' part of the hypothesis?

Consider the moments when a tentative reservation is accepted, expires, or becomes part of a valid gang commit, and ask whether two incompatible assignments can ever take effect for the same resource. The difficult cases are delayed actions from a stale epoch, a commit in progress as expiry occurs, and workers reaching different local conclusions about the gang. Epoch fencing and expiry need consistent rules across those cases; the absence of an observed conflict in an uncomplicated case would not establish the general claim.
Could a worker safely wait past five seconds if it is uncertain whether a commit occurred?

Waiting would avoid a premature release, but it would also affect the proposed claim that uncommitted reservations expire after five seconds and orphaned holds clear within ten seconds. The hypothesis needs a way to distinguish genuine uncertainty from an uncommitted hold that is safe to expire. It should not quietly trade away either its timing claim or its no-conflict claim when that distinction is difficult.
So the hypothesis hinges on what 'expire' means, not just on a timer firing?

Exactly. A timer firing can initiate a decision, but safe expiry means the reservation can no longer become an effective claim that conflicts with reuse of the resource. The worker must interpret late messages consistently with that decision. For a gang, expiry also has to remain consistent with whether the overall attempt validly committed.
Can I describe epoch fencing as the reason the expired reservation can't come back?

You can describe that as the intended role of epoch fencing in the hypothesis. To make it a demonstrated reason, the design would have to show that all relevant stale actions are rejected, including any delayed action that could make an expired reservation effective. It must also show how a worker treats actions whose timing overlaps expiry, rather than relying on the label 'fenced' to resolve the overlap.
What's the narrowest accurate statement I can make now?

The hypothesis is that epoch-fenced workers can expire uncommitted gang-ID reservations after five seconds, clearing orphaned holds within ten seconds without conflicting assignments. It has not yet established when those intervals begin, how workers conclusively identify an uncommitted attempt, or how expiry interacts with a commit already in progress. Those are the points that determine whether the timing and safety claims hold together.
I plan to run GangFault-1k mid-commit partition tests and verify stale-epoch rejection, orphan-hold clearance within ten seconds, and zero duplicate allocations. How should I frame that plan?

Frame it as a test plan, not as a result. GangFault-1k will exercise partitions during gang commits. The checks are whether actions from stale epochs are rejected, whether orphaned holds clear within ten seconds, and whether the tests observe zero duplicate allocations. Those checks focus on the safety and cleanup questions raised by a scheduler losing its lease mid-commit.
What makes the mid-commit timing important?

A partition in the middle of a gang commit can leave some resource claims acknowledged while the gang's overall outcome remains uncertain. That creates an opportunity for a stale scheduler action to arrive late, for a hold to remain after it is no longer needed, or for a resource to be allocated twice during cleanup. Testing that moment probes how the design handles partial reservations rather than only completed placements.
Does the name GangFault-1k tell us how many faults or jobs to run?

The plan names the tests GangFault-1k, but it does not define what “1k” counts. It would be inaccurate to infer a run count, job count, or fault count from the name alone. You can retain the name while specifying the test scope separately when that information is available.
For stale-epoch rejection, should I check only that the scheduler knows its epoch is old?

No. The relevant check is whether an action from a stale epoch can become effective where an assignment or reservation is enforced. A scheduler recognizing that it is stale is useful, but it does not establish rejection of a delayed action already on its way to a worker. The test should make the acceptance or rejection of such actions observable without assuming that an old message simply disappears.
Would rejecting a new reservation from the stale epoch cover the issue?

It would cover one case, but the mid-commit case also raises the question of actions concerning reservations that already exist. A late action must not turn an old tentative claim into an effective assignment that conflicts with a newer one. Stale-epoch rejection should therefore be assessed at every action relevant to making an allocation effective, not only when a reservation is first requested.
How can I tell whether a hold is an orphan for the clearance check?

The test needs a definition grounded in the gang attempt's outcome. A hold is not necessarily orphaned just because one worker has not heard that the gang committed; the outcome could still be uncertain from that worker's perspective. For the ten-second check, identify holds that are no longer needed for a valid commit, then determine when they cease to block reuse. Otherwise the test might count a premature release as successful cleanup.
Where should the ten-second clock begin?

The plan states clearance within ten seconds but does not specify the starting event. That needs to be defined before running the check. In particular, the time a partition is introduced, the time a scheduler loses its lease, the time a hold is established to be orphaned, and the time connectivity stabilizes are not interchangeable by default. The reported clearance interval should say which event starts it and what observable event marks its end.
What should count as the end of orphan-hold clearance?

A useful endpoint is when the orphaned claim no longer prevents a safe new allocation of its resource and cannot be revived by a stale action. Merely deleting a local record may not demonstrate that. The plan's ten-second check needs an observable release condition consistent with the no-duplicate-allocation check.
Does zero duplicate allocations mean no two schedulers ever propose the same resource?

The central safety concern is conflicting effective assignments, not merely competing proposals.
