The plan does not prescribe instrumentation, but the allocation measurement needs to reflect what actually takes effect.
What if a scheduler proposes an assignment using a token that a worker rejects?

A rejected proposal is not a duplicate allocation if it never becomes effective. It can be useful evidence that validation was exercised, but the duplicate-allocation measure must distinguish rejected attempts from incompatible effective assignments.
And what if two schedulers both think they can assign the same resource?

Their beliefs or proposals do not alone constitute a conflict. The safety question is whether token validation and the applicable gang decisions permit two incompatible assignments to become effective for that resource. Partition replays should make that distinction observable, including for delayed actions from a scheduler acting on an outdated view.
Does a logged gang decision make every worker learn the outcome at once?

No. Workers may learn a logged outcome at different times. The implementation must keep an uncertain worker from treating a potentially committed slot as free merely because it has not yet learned the decision. Conversely, it should not activate a gang merely on the basis of one worker’s tentative claim.
Should the replays include partitions while a gang decision is being established?

That is a particularly relevant conceptual case because partial reservations and delayed knowledge of a gang outcome can threaten assignment safety. The plan says to replay partitions, however, without specifying which traces, how many events, or exactly when each partition occurs. An execution record should identify the cases it actually exercises rather than treating a suggested case as already specified.
Do I need to replay a particular number of partitions or use a particular worker count?

Neither is specified in this plan. It names the implementation work, partition replay, and the measurements, but gives no replay count or worker count. Those parameters should be recorded when the replay is defined; they should not be inferred from the plan’s wording.
What counts as a duplicate allocation in the replay?

Two incompatible assignments becoming effective for the same resource. A tentative hold, a proposal, and a rejected action should remain distinguishable from an effective allocation. A transient duplicate still counts even if cleanup later leaves only one assignment, so observing only the final state would not capture the whole safety outcome.
Could a gang fail to activate without causing a duplicate allocation?

Yes. An incomplete or unresolved gang attempt is not itself a duplicate allocation. It can nevertheless block resources and affect recovery or tenant wait. That is one reason to measure progress and waiting separately from allocation conflicts.
What does 'recovery within 30 seconds' mean in this plan?

It refers to restoration of scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. The clock should not silently begin when the partition starts or when an individual worker first reconnects. The replay also needs an observable event that counts as scheduling progress, rather than treating token validation, a logged decision, or reservation cleanup alone as sufficient.
Would making an authorized token available count as recovered scheduling?

Not necessarily. A token may enable a later assignment, but progress requires an actual scheduling advance consistent with the gang’s placement constraints and activation decision. The measurement should not end simply because a prerequisite is in place if scheduling still cannot move forward.
Does the 30-second condition mean all gang jobs have to start within that period?

No. It concerns restoring scheduling progress after connectivity stabilizes, not a start-time deadline for every queued gang. Progress must remain safe, and tenant fairness still matters, but the 30-second interval should not be reinterpreted as a universal job-wait limit.
Could the replay show safe allocations but fail to demonstrate recovery?

Yes. A system could avoid conflicting assignments by leaving uncertain resources unavailable yet fail to make scheduling progress in time. Duplicate allocations and recovery latency are separate measurements in the plan precisely so that safety is not mistaken for liveness.
Could it show recovery within 30 seconds while recording a duplicate?

It could show scheduling activity quickly while also revealing an incompatible allocation. That would not make the safety concern disappear. The plan measures both outcomes independently; quick recovery cannot excuse a duplicate assignment.
How do placement constraints affect the recovery measurement?

A scheduler cannot demonstrate a valid gang placement by assigning an arbitrary set of available workers. The replay must distinguish delay due to scheduling recovery from the absence of any feasible placement under the applicable constraints. The plan does not specify particular constraints or a workload, so those conditions must be clear when interpreting a measured recovery time.
What should feasible-tenant wait measure?

It should measure the time applicable tenant demand remains waiting while it is considered feasible under the scheduling and gang-placement rules. The plan does not specify the wait-clock start and end events, or whether it will report a maximum, distribution, or another statistic. Those choices need to be explicit so the recorded wait can be interpreted.
Is a tenant’s demand feasible just because its priority has increased?

No. A fairness signal cannot manufacture a placement. Feasibility must account for a compatible gang placement and any preemption the scheduler actually permits, while respecting resources whose claims remain uncertain or committed. The wait measure should not relabel infeasible demand as feasible solely because it has waited longer.
If feasible demand is still waiting when a replay ends, should I omit it from tenant-wait measurements?

No. Omitting an unfinished wait could make the reported waiting behavior misleading. Its unresolved status and elapsed time should remain visible under whatever reporting convention is chosen. This plan does not specify such a convention or report any observed tenant waits.
Does a finite tenant-wait measurement prove starvation is impossible?

No. It describes waiting observed during the replay. Preventing starvation under feasible demand is a broader requirement: feasible demand must not be bypassed indefinitely as scheduling proceeds. Measured waits can inform that assessment, but a finite replay alone does not establish a universal guarantee.
Should I treat activation safety and fair preemption as one combined measurement?

Keep them distinct while examining their interaction. Token validation and logged gang decisions govern whether resource claims and gang activation are safe. Fairness and placement-aware preemption influence which feasible demand is served and when. An unsafe release to reduce waiting would not satisfy the allocation requirement, while perfectly safe activation would not by itself prevent long tenant waits.
What should a report from these replays avoid claiming before values are available?

It should not say there were zero duplicates, that progress returned within 30 seconds, or that feasible tenants avoided starvation. Nor should it invent a replay count, worker count, token protocol, or gang-decision format. For now, those are implementation subjects and outcomes to measure.

What exactly should count as reconciliation of a hold?

A meaningful completion is an established status with safe consequences. A hold belonging to a valid committed gang remains protected; a claim that cannot be part of a valid commitment becomes safely available for reuse. Merely starting a lookup, receiving a shard lease, or deleting a local record would not necessarily establish that the hold has been reconciled.
Does the 25-second target require all committed holds to be released?

No. The proposal calls for reconciling holds within 25 seconds after reconnection, not freeing every held resource. Retaining a hold that supports a valid committed gang can be the correct reconciled outcome. The timing question concerns reaching and applying the correct outcome, including safe release of claims that should not remain.

Those choices would change the measured interval. An evaluation should state its starting event rather than assume that every shard reconnects together.
Could the scheduler claim it met 25 seconds by timing only the first hold that gets resolved?

That would not answer whether stranded holds delayed reconciliation beyond 25 seconds. The measurement needs to cover the relevant holds left by the cross-rack attempt and identify when each reaches a settled, safe state. An early resolution on one shard cannot stand in for unresolved claims on another.
If the last hold is resolved at exactly 25 seconds after the defined reconnection event, is that within the target?

Yes. “Within 25 seconds” ordinarily includes completion at the 25-second boundary. A relevant hold still unresolved after that boundary would not meet the proposed timing, assuming the starting and completion events have been defined consistently.
Could one shard keep its hold while another releases its hold, without causing a conflict?

Their local states may differ temporarily while they learn the gang-wide outcome. Whether that particular combination is safe depends on what outcome was established and whether either released resource can be assigned incompatibly. The design must prevent a released portion from conflicting with a valid committed gang, while not treating a remaining tentative portion as a complete active placement.
What is the main safety condition during that temporary disagreement?

No resource involved in the uncertain cross-rack attempt may receive incompatible effective assignments. A stale lease holder, a delayed gang action, and a worker with incomplete knowledge must all be unable to turn a supposedly released claim into a conflict. That condition applies while the attempt is being reconciled, not just after all records agree.
Would avoiding conflict by blocking every shard until every hold is resolved answer the question?

It could be a conservative safety response, but it would not answer the timing part unless the relevant holds were reconciled within 25 seconds after reconnection. The question asks whether atomic cross-rack authority and prompt resolution can coexist. Indefinitely blocking resources avoids some unsafe reuse while leaving the stranded-hold concern unresolved.
Could a placement on an unrelated, reconciled shard proceed meanwhile?

Conceptually, it could if its authority and resource claims are established and it does not depend on the uncertain cross-rack resources. The open question does not prescribe a global pause. But progress elsewhere would not show that the stranded holds from this cross-rack gang were reconciled within 25 seconds.
How do placement constraints complicate deciding whether a partial hold is harmless?

A cross-rack gang needs a compatible collection of resources. Holding some of them may block another feasible placement even if those resources are not enough to activate the original gang. Equally, releasing one portion does not necessarily make the remaining workers a valid placement. The design has to evaluate the gang-wide outcome and the claims on actual resources rather than infer feasibility from a count of available slots.
Could tenant deficit aging justify taking an uncertain hold away sooner?

No. A tenant’s growing deficit may affect scheduling priority, but it does not establish that an uncertain claim can safely be reassigned. Reconciliation first has to determine whether the hold belongs to a valid committed gang or can be released without conflict. Fairness decisions then operate on resources whose status is known and on placements that satisfy the constraints.
Does resolving the holds within 25 seconds show that scheduling progress returns within 30 seconds?

Not by itself. Hold reconciliation is one possible prerequisite for placing work; scheduling progress also needs valid authority and a feasible placement. The proposal phrases the 25-second condition after reconnection, while the separate progress requirement is within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. Those starting conditions and outcomes should not be silently equated.

Does the quorum log settle the status of a hold without any worker-side checks?

It can provide an authoritative gang-wide outcome, but workers still need to act consistently with that outcome. Does this hypothesis assert zero duplicate allocations as well?

Not explicitly. It predicts timely release of incomplete cross-rack shard holds without activating partial gangs. No. A coordinator could prevent all activation while leaving incomplete holds unresolved. The two parts must be examined separately: whether any partial gang becomes active, and when every qualifying incomplete hold is safely released relative to a defined starting event.
